systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, and María Micaela Sviatschi
NBER Working Paper No. 35986
November 2026
JEL No. O10, P0
ABSTRACT
Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet 
little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among 
incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates 
under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized 
controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers 
to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, 
designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months 
after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and 
stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized 
victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less 
likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative 
records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased 
GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive 
evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers 
working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female 
officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings 
show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how 
incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the 
broader workplace environment.

1 Introduction
Improving the performance of frontline bureaucracies is central to building effective states (Besley
and Persson, 2009; Page and Pande, 2018). Existing research has emphasized the role of personnel
selection, incentives, and accountability in determining the quality of public services (e.g., Duflo
et al., 2012; Das et al., 2016; Finan et al., 2017). However, even when bureaucrats operate under the
same formal rules and incentives, frontline interactions often require substantial discretion, and
differences in officials’ attitudes, beliefs, and decision-making can shape the quality of services
citizens receive. Whether these attributes can be changed among incumbent state agents and
whether doing so improves their interactions with citizens, remains less well understood.
Law enforcement provides a particularly consequential setting in which to study this question.
Police officers routinely make high-stakes decisions about whether to take complaints seriously,
initiate formal procedures, and provide citizens with access to legal protections (Dube et al., 2025;
Amaral et al., 2025). Moreover, unlike many other public services, policing has no close private
substitute: the state retains a monopoly over the application of the law. Biases in the exercise of
police discretion can therefore restrict access to justice and weaken citizens’ willingness to engage
with the state.
These concerns are especially salient for gender-based violence (GBV), which is characterized
by stigma, fear of backlash, and forms of victimization that are frequently concealed from public
scrutiny (Murvartian et al., 2024). In this case, dismissive responses, victim-blaming, and proce-
dural barriers at police stations reduce reporting and perpetuate inequality in legal protection.1 In
response to these challenges, policymakers have turned to gender quotas which have increased
reporting crimes against women (Miller and Segal, 2019; Sukhtankar et al., 2022; Amaral et al.,
2021; Sviatschi and Trako, 2024; García-Hombrados et al., 2024; Asik et al., 2026; Bernhardt et al.,
2026). Yet policing remains a male-dominated and highly hierarchical profession, in which senior
officers exercise substantial discretion and tenure protections limit the scope for personnel real-
location.2 These institutional features raise a central question: can the attitudes and behavior of

institutional failure. Prior work shows that police officers’ attitudes toward GBV, such as beliefs about victim credi-
bility or whether sexual harassment merits police action, strongly shape officers’ behavior and affect crime incidence
(Amaral et al., 2025)
2In India, several states have adopted gender quotas in law enforcement. However, female recruitment remains
low, and quota thresholds are often not met (Tata Trusts, 2023). Qualitative evidence further suggests that female

existing state agents be reshaped, and does doing so improve the services citizens receive?
This paper studies whether reshaping GBV attitudes and skills of senior police officers through
a novel expressive arts intervention can improve policing performance and the workplace envi-
ronment in the presence of entrenched gender bias. To study this question, we partner with the
Bihar Police in India, to implement a clustered randomized controlled trial covering 417 police
stations across twelve districts and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers serving
42 million citizens. Bihar is the poorest state in India, and provides a particularly relevant con-
text: despite recent legislative improvements, gender violence remains highly prevalent, report-
ing rates are extremely low, and women remain underrepresented in decision-making roles within
police stations.3 Our intervention targets key decision-makers— Station House Officers, Inspec-
tors, Sub-Inspectors, and Assistant Sub-Inspectors—who shape both citizen-facing behavior and
internal workplace norms.4
Motivated by evidence that immersive and experiential learning can be more effective than
traditional instruction in shifting beliefs, norms, and decision-making in high-discretion settings
(Andries et al., 2024; Dube et al., 2025; Ashraf et al., 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025), we design a
novel expressive arts-based training tailored to address police biases towards GBV in India. The
intervention was informed by 18 months of qualitative fieldwork, including sustained observa-
tion in police stations and interviews with officers, GBV survivors, and civil society organizations.
This fieldwork highlighted two features of the police organization that shaped the program de-
sign: substantial discretion in officers’ responses to GBV and a highly hierarchical workplace in
which senior officers influence both case handling and norms of appropriate conduct.
The intervention therefore targets senior active duty field officers and combines perspective-
remaining in the police force. Moreover, most quotas apply to lower-ranking positions within police stations, limiting
women’s representation in decision-making roles. Indeed, Bernhardt et al. (2026) show experimentally that assigning
female constables to police stations increases GBV registration while, at the same time, male colleagues become more
likely to express biased beliefs about female complainants. This tension points to a distinct challenge: improving
representation may expand women’s access to the state without changing—and may in some cases reinforce—the
beliefs through which incumbent male officers exercise discretion.
3According to the Bihar Economic Survey 2025-26, Bihar’s per capita remains the lowest in India with a per capita
GDP at current prices of USD 925. Bihar’s GDP is comparable to those of other low-income countries such as Sierra
Leone, Uganda, or Gambia.
4Reforming the police has been a persistent challenge in Bihar. GBV remains widespread: 40 percent of women
aged 18–49 report having experienced spousal physical or sexual violence, yet only 2 percent of survivors seek help
from the police (NFHS-5, 2022, 2021). This gap persists despite the existence of formal legal protections against
domestic violence and a 35 percent gender quota in police recruitment (Tata Trusts, 2023). Moreover, women remain
underrepresented in decision-making roles within police stations, limiting their influence over frontline responses to
GBV.
2
taking, experiential learning, and collective reflection. It draws on Freirean conscientization (Freire,
1970) and Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed (Boal, 2014), adapting these methods to policing and of-
ficers’ interactions with GBV survivors. Through role play and simulated police-station scenar-
ios, officers assume the perspectives of survivors and responding officers, confront competing
interpretations of the same situation, and collectively reflect on appropriate responses. Rather
than prescribing a single behavioral rule, the training exposes officers to context-rich scenarios in
which they must exercise judgment, with the aim of improving how they interpret situations and
use discretion. Guided reflection, peer feedback, and explicit commitments to station-level prac-
tice changes reinforce these experiences and create shared expectations about acceptable conduct
(Bicchieri, 2016).
We hypothesize that the intervention operates through two reinforcing channels. First, it
changes how officers interpret situations and exercise discretion by fostering perspective-taking
and empathy (individual attitudes channel). Second, because the training is delivered collectively
and publicly to senior officers from multiple stations, it creates shared experiences and expecta-
tions about appropriate conduct, potentially reshaping workplace norms and diffusing through
the police hierarchy (workplace channel). We use plausibly exogenous officer transfers to explore
the importance of these channels.5
Our analysis draws on a rich set of newly collected data that captures officer attitudes, be-
havior, and workplace dynamics using surveys, random victims’ audit data, and administrative
police records. We measure police officers’ mindsets, attitudes, and technical skills related to
GBV using detailed novel survey measures administered to senior male officers. We make use
of self-reported measures, along with vignettes, thus, taking into account possible measurement
concerns (Bursztyn et al., 2025). To measure real-world policing behavior, we implement a stan-
dardized victim audit in which trained decoys visit police stations to lodge complaints and sys-
tematically record officers’ responses, and we complement these measures with administrative
data on crime registration and handling drawn from approximately 500,000 official police records.
To assess changes in the workplace environment and potential spillovers, we conducted confiden-
tial surveys of junior female constables at treated and control police stations. These officers were

because the training was designed and delivered as a single integrated program rather than as separable modules. We
therefore rely on plausibly exogenous officer transfers to distinguish patterns consistent with persistent individual-

not targeted by the intervention, allowing us to measure whether the intervention affected their
experiences of harassment, anxiety, and perceptions of senior officers. In addition, we use data on
officer transfers to examine the mechanisms underlying the intervention’s effects and the extent
to which those effects spillover to untreated officers. Together, these data allow us to link changes
in officer attitudes to downstream changes in workplace culture and service delivery.
We find that immersive expressive-arts training significantly improves police attitudes and
thus, performance, workplace environment, and interactions with survivors of GBV. In particular,
we find that treated senior officers exhibit greater empathy, stronger beliefs in the credibility of
survivors’ complaints, and greater legal and procedural knowledge. Approximately one year
after the intervention, standardized victim audits show that these changes are accompanied by
substantial improvements in real-world police behavior: officers are less likely to dismiss cases or
blame victims and more likely to provide appropriate guidance and referrals.
Consistent with these behavioral changes, administrative data show that officers in treated
police stations register GBV cases more quickly following reported incidents, indicating improved
responsiveness in formalizing complaints. We also find that treated officers devote more time to
investigating and following up on GBV cases. Furthermore, after one year, we observe an increase
in the overall volume of GBV First Information Reports (FIRs). Importantly, this increase emerges
only after earlier improvements in officer attitudes, behavior, and responsiveness, a sequence
consistent with improved service delivery increasing victims’ willingness to seek help and engage
with the justice system.
We also provide suggestive evidence on the mechanisms underlying these effects. We exploit
officer transfers across police stations, which are frequent in the Indian bureaucracy (Iyer and
Mani, 2012), to examine whether the effects persist with treated officers and diffuse to untreated
colleagues.6 Treated officers who move to control stations retain improvements in GBV attitudes,
consistent with a persistent individual-level change that survives a change in workplace envi-
ronment. At the same time, untreated officers who move into treated stations exhibit sizable
improvements, consistent with exposure to treated peers and station-level norm diffusion. Taken
together, these patterns suggest that the intervention operates through a combination of durable
6Transfers are not randomly assigned. They are common in the Indian bureaucracy and often occur for adminis-
trative reasons, but they may also reflect political considerations, disciplinary actions, officer requests, or responses
to major incidents. We therefore interpret the transfer analysis as suggestive evidence on persistence and diffusion
rather than as a source of exogenous variation.
4
individual change and changes in workplace norms.
The effects also extend beyond directly treated officers to the broader workplace environment.
Eight months after the training, junior female officers stationed with treated senior officers report
significantly lower levels of workplace harassment and anxiety, suggesting that changes in senior
officers’ behavior affect not only their interactions with GBV survivors but also how senior officers
exercise authority within the police organization.
Several pieces of evidence make alternative explanations based on changes in formal incen-
tives, sample composition, social desirability, or short-run monitoring less likely. First, the in-
tervention did not alter officers’ formal responsibilities, compensation, promotion prospects, or
enforcement intensity, making explanations based on changes in formal incentives less likely.
Second, results are robust to controlling for the share of female officers, and social desirability
measures.7 The fact that we also detect changes in performance using audit data, and among
non-treated officers (females and non-treated transferred officers) further reassures that results
are not driven by these measurement concerns. Third, we also find that treatment effects do
not vary with officers’ rank or hierarchical position, which would be expected if changes were
primarily driven by senior officers rewarding visible compliance. Moreover, key outcomes are
measured well after the training—approximately one year later in the standardized victim audits
and over an even longer horizon in the administrative records. The audits capture behavior in
settings where officers were unaware of being evaluated, while the administrative records are
generated independently of the research team, reducing concerns about short-run signaling or
experimenter demand effects. Together, these patterns support an interpretation in which the in-
tervention operates through shifts in officer attitudes and decision-making rather than through
mechanical channels.
This paper contributes to the literature on public service delivery (e.g., Finan et al., 2017; Ra-
sul and Rogger, 2018) and frontline workers (Maynard-Moody and Musheno, 2003) by providing
causal evidence that an intervention targeting attitudes, and decision-making among state agents
can improve performance in a high-discretion institutional setting. Prior work on policing shows
how officers’ decision making is affected by their attitudes and prevalent social norms (Amaral
et al., 2025), but there is limited evidence on whether interventions can generate persistent be-
7As we will explain, our novel measures include a mix of direct-questioning and vignettes – tools designed to
mitigate concerns over desirability bias (Bursztyn et al., 2025).
5
havioral change among frontline bureaucrats or service providers – key agents in GBV response.
We show that an immersive, experiential training targeting senior police officers significantly im-
proves both attitudes and real-world behavior toward victims of GBV. Thereby establishing a
direct link between bias reduction and service quality in a core state function. Unlike reforms that
rely on changing personnel composition or creating parallel institutions, our intervention oper-
ates within the existing hierarchy, targeting decision-makers who shape both case outcomes and
workplace norms. The results suggest that attitudes, norms and institutional culture are integral
components of public sector performance. More broadly, by targeting senior officers within hi-
erarchical police stations, we complement recent work on the role of public-sector managers in
shaping the performance of government agencies (Fenizia, 2022). Our findings suggest that man-
agers may influence not only organizational performance and worker effort, but also workplace
norms, discretionary behavior, and the treatment of vulnerable citizens.
Second, we contribute to the experimental literature on police training (Dube et al., 2025; Bern-
hardt et al., 2026; Harris et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2021; Canales et al., 2025). Closely related, Dube
et al. (2025) show that experiential training can induce a “cognitive pause” in high-stress policing
environments and reduce use of force. We build on this work by studying a different source of
discretionary failure: gender bias in officers’ interactions with survivors of GBV. We show that
experiential training can generate persistent changes in attitudes and service quality. We further
combine survey measures with standardized victim audits and administrative records, allowing
us to trace effects from individual attitudes to real-world police behavior as well as quantifying
spillover effects on untreated officers.
Finally, we contribute to the literature on gender norms, perspective-taking, and experien-
tial learning (e.g., Dhar et al., 2022; Sharma, 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025; Banerjee et al., 2019;
Andries et al., 2024; Ashraf et al., 2024). This literature shows that narratives, curricula, and par-
ticipatory interventions can shift attitudes. Most closely related, Chaudhuri et al. (2025) study
Jana Sanskriti’s community-based participatory theater in West Bengal and find changes in the
acceptability of domestic violence and women’s voice. We bring these insights into a markedly
different institutional setting: a hierarchical state bureaucracy in which participants themselves
exercise substantial authority over citizens. Rather than seeking to change norms among citizens,
our intervention seeks to change how incumbent state agents interpret situations and exercise
discretion. Our setting allows us to study whether experiential methods designed to challenge
deeply rooted social norms can alter the behavior of state agents, whether these changes persist,

6.4.2 Organizational Spillovers and Workplace Culture
If the intervention altered station-level norms or supervisory practices, its effects may extend
beyond treated officers to colleagues who did not participate in the intervention. We examine this
possibility using outcomes for female constables, none of whom received the intervention directly.
Whether training programs can generate broader changes in organizational culture remains far
from established, particularly in public-sector settings.18 Table 6 shows a test of whether the
intervention affected the workplace environment experienced by non-treated officers.

retaining women in a heavily male-dominated institution, fostering a more gender-equal police
force both in the immediate term but also in terms of the pipeline of officers.
7 Cost and Benchmarking
The training curriculum and its delivery were funded by the Fund for Innovation in Develop-
ment (FID), separately from the accompanying research and evaluation activities (officer surveys,
standardized victim audits, and administrative data collection), which were funded through the
J-PAL Crime and Violence Initiative and the J-PAL Gender Initiative.20 The cost of delivering the
intervention was EUR 136,560 (USD 151,600), approximately USD 108 per officer trained and USD
699 per treated station. The 217 treated stations serve an estimated 21.8 million residents; spread
across that population, the one-time delivery cost is under one US cent per resident. The training
is a one-time investment in officers, but its potential benefits extend to the much larger population
these officers serve.
At USD 108 per officer and an estimated effect of 0.082 standard deviations on the GBV at-
titudes index, the implied cost is approximately USD 1,320 per standard deviation of attitude
change. This is a cost-effectiveness metric rather than a welfare metric: it relates program cost di-
rectly to measured impact without requiring a monetary valuation of changes in GBV outcomes.
If these effects persist, this one-time cost is more appropriately expressed on an annualized basis:
USD 108 per officer if the effects last only one year, falling to as little as USD 22 per officer per
year if they persist for five. Appendix E reports these calculations under alternative persistence
assumptions.
To our knowledge, no published study reports both the cost and the impact of a police-focused
psychological well-being. We find no detectable effects on either depression (PHQ-9) or anxiety (GAD-7), suggesting
that improvements in GBV-related attitudes and behavior were not accompanied by deterioration in these dimensions
of officers’ mental health.

gender-based-violence training program specifically: the closest police intervention, the Women’s
Help Desk reform evaluated by Sukhtankar et al. (2022), is a bundled reform rather than a stand-
alone training and does not report costs on a comparable basis. This limits the scope for bench-
marking on a common cost basis. Our intervention produces effects at three levels: officers’ atti-
tudes and technical skills, their case-handling behavior in standardized audits, and administrative
case registration. No single external study speaks to all three, so we benchmark each against the
closest available evidence (Appendix E reports the full comparison).
On cost, the program is inexpensive in absolute terms, approximately USD 108 per officer
for a three-day training with follow-up and monitoring. The closest comparator that is itself a
behavioral training for serving police and reports both cost and field impact, the 16-hour Sit-D
program in Chicago, which cut uses of force and discretionary arrests by about 23 percent, cost
USD 807 to 864 per officer trained (Dube et al., 2025); we do not read the gap as a like-for-like
efficiency comparison, since cross-country training costs are dominated by local wage levels. On
attitudes, the training’s effect on officers’ GBV attitudes was on the order of half the standardized
effect of a 2.5-year, 28-session gender-attitudes curriculum for adolescents in India, a population
generally taken to be more malleable and reached over far more contact time (Dhar et al., 2022);
because the two indices measure different attitudes, this comparison is only approximate. On the
behavioral and administrative outcomes of most direct policy relevance, the closest comparator
is again Sukhtankar et al. (2022), which raised the number of women’s cases formally registered.
Our training moved that same registration margin, raising GBV reporting over the longer run,
and additionally reduced the delay between a reported incident and its registration by 41 percent,
a margin that study did not examine.
Beyond cost, the intervention’s significance lies in where its measured effects sit in the broader
chain from policing to women’s welfare. The attitudes, case-handling, and registration outcomes
we document are the proximate margins through which frontline policing shapes whether women
seek and obtain redress. More effective redress can, in turn, alter women’s perceived risks from
participating in public life and reduce the need for costly avoidance responses. A companion
police experiment in Hyderabad makes this downstream link concrete: where uniformed patrols
reduced severe public-space sexual harassment, women became roughly 30 percent less likely
to move elsewhere in response to it, easing constraints on physical mobility that are linked to
women’s schooling (Borker, ming) and labor force participation. Such changes can affect la-
bor supply on both the extensive margin—whether women work at all—and the intensive mar-
35
gin—where, when, and how much they work. In Hyderabad, police visibility and officers’ at-
titudes toward harassment were central to the effect (Amaral et al., 2025), the same attitudinal
margin targeted by our intervention. A training that improves these attitudes and the quality of
redress at modest cost may therefore have consequences that extend beyond police performance
to women’s willingness to take risks, participate in public spaces, and pursue economic opportu-
nities, even where we do not attach a dollar value to these downstream benefits.
8 Conclusion
Public institutions frequently fail citizens not only because of limited resources or weak incentives,
but also because of the beliefs and biases of the frontline agents who deliver the state’s services.
Policing makes this especially consequential. Officers exercise substantial discretion over which
complaints are registered, how survivors are treated, and whether the law is applied consistently.
Unlike most public services, policing has no private substitute. When this discretion is shaped by
entrenched gender norms, access to justice becomes unequal precisely for those who depend on
the state most.
This paper asks whether the performance of an existing, hierarchical, and male-dominated
police force can be improved by reshaping the attitudes and skills of the officers who already staff
it. Partnering with the Government of Bihar, we implemented a clustered randomized evaluation
of a three-day expressive arts curriculum, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, delivered
to senior officers in 417 police stations. Approximately 7 months after the baseline, treated of-
ficers exhibit significant improvements in attitudes toward GBV, higher empathy, and stronger
legal and procedural knowledge. These gains translate into real-world behavior. Standardized
victim audits conducted roughly one year later show that treated officers are less likely to dismiss
complaints or blame survivors and more likely to provide appropriate guidance and referrals,
and administrative records show that stations register cases substantially more quickly after an
incident occurs. Over a longer horizon, reports of GBV rise in treated stations, consistent with
improved police responsiveness increasing survivors’ willingness to seek help.
Beyond documenting that bias among state agents is malleable, the paper provides evidence
on how change emerges and why it persists. Exploiting plausibly exogenous officer transfers, we
show that treated officers continue to improve after moving to stations where no peer was trained,
36
while untreated officers improve after moving into treated stations. Together with lower reported
harassment and anxiety among junior female constables, who were never targeted by the inter-
vention, these patterns point to two reinforcing channels: durable individual-level change in how
officers interpret situations and exercise discretion, and the diffusion of new norms through the
station hierarchy. The sequence of effects is itself informative. Improvements in officer attitudes,
conduct, and responsiveness appear first, while increases in citizen reporting emerge only with a
lag, consistent with better service delivery gradually rebuilding trust rather than with mechanical
compliance or short-run experimenter demand.
These findings speak to a central question in the study of state capacity. Whereas many re-
forms seek to improve service delivery by changing who provides it, through female recruitment,
gender quotas, specialized courts, or dedicated women’s police stations, we show that the behav-
ior of the officers already in place can be reshaped from within. This distinction matters in set-
tings where governments struggle to recruit and retain women despite formal quotas, and where
tenure protections limit personnel reallocation. By targeting senior officers who shape both case
outcomes and workplace norms, the intervention operates on the decision-makers whose discre-
tion is most consequential for survivors.
More broadly, our results suggest that improving governance may require addressing the so-
cial and organizational foundations of bureaucratic behavior. Citizens do not experience the state
in the abstract; they experience it through a single interaction with a frontline official, and the
quality of that interaction can determine whether the law reaches them at all. Interventions that
cultivate perspective-taking and reshape workplace norms can change how those interactions
unfold, generating durable improvements in the treatment of vulnerable citizens and offering a
scalable path to strengthening state capacity in high-discretion institutional settings.
